PRODUCT DESIGN CASE STUDY

Horal

Live product · Web + iOS + Android

Horal

Horal made me think hard about trust. A buyer needs to feel safe sending money, and a seller needs the tools to do their job. I worked on both sides.

MY ROLEEnd-to-end product designer · mobile app + website
STATUSLive product · 2026
FOCUSMarketplace trust, escrow, KYC, buyer journeys, seller operations
PROBLEM

Buyers need enough confidence to transact with independent sellers they may not know, while sellers still need serious operational tools behind the transaction.

MY OWNERSHIP

End-to-end product design across the mobile app and website, covering buyer journeys, seller operations and the shared marketplace system.

KEY CONSTRAINT

Make verification, escrow and KYC visible enough to build trust without making shopping feel defensive or exposing seller-side complexity to buyers.

OUTCOME / PROOF

Live on the web, iOS and Android. Public listings document escrow, KYC, chat, seller inventory, orders, wallet and payout capabilities.

IF YOU HAVE ONE MINUTE

Here’s the decision I kept coming back to.

A marketplace can look lovely and still make someone nervous about paying a stranger.

What I chose

I treated verification and escrow as parts of the actual shopping journey, not as reassuring slogans.

What you can see

The shipped product includes verification, escrow, chat and seller tools, documented in its public listings.

What stayed with me

Designing for trust also meant designing what the seller sees after an order arrives.

01The short version

Horal is a live Nigerian multi-vendor marketplace designed to make buying from independent sellers safer and more transparent. I owned the product design end to end across the mobile app and website, shaping the experience from discovery and product evaluation through checkout, escrow, communication and post-purchase confidence, while also designing the seller side needed to list products, manage stock, fulfil orders and receive payouts.

02What I owned

I designed the customer and seller journeys as one connected marketplace system: browsing and search, product and store presentation, trust signals, checkout, escrow status, in-app communication, seller onboarding and KYC, product listing and inventory variants, order management, store profile and location, seller wallet and earnings, and the responsive website experience around the product.

03The challenge

A marketplace has a trust problem before it has a checkout problem. The buyer needs enough confidence to pay someone they may not know, while the seller needs tools that make fulfilment, inventory and payout manageable enough to keep the marketplace reliable. The design therefore had to make safety visible without making every screen feel defensive, and give sellers operational depth without exposing that complexity to shoppers.

04The product model

The buyer experience is organised around confidence: find the right product, understand who is selling it, communicate when necessary, pay with protection, then see what happens next. The seller experience follows the same order from the other side: establish identity, create the store, list and manage products, receive an order, fulfil it, and track earnings and payouts. Escrow sits between those two journeys as the system that lets both sides move forward.

05Decision stories

01 / TRUST SIGNALS

Make verification part of the buying decision.

Problem
A buyer is deciding whether to trust a seller they may never have met.
Constraint
Safety needs to be visible without making every screen feel suspicious or compliance-heavy.
Decision
Verification became a visible marketplace signal tied to the store rather than a hidden back-office check.
Evidence
Store verification and KYC are shipping capabilities documented in the live app listings.
02 / ESCROW

Turn escrow into a journey, not a badge.

Problem
A payment badge does not tell either side what is happening to the money after checkout.
Constraint
Buyer confidence and seller fulfilment need to stay connected without exposing financial complexity.
Decision
Designed explicit states from payment protected to order moving, delivery confirmed and funds released.
Evidence
Google Play documents escrow-protected transactions in the live product.
03 / COMMUNICATION

Keep questions inside the protected transaction.

Problem
Product and fulfilment questions are inevitable before and after payment.
Constraint
Moving the conversation to another app breaks context and weakens the protected marketplace journey.
Decision
Chat became part of commerce rather than a separate support feature.
Evidence
In-app chat with image sharing is included in the shipping product notes.
04 / SELLER OPERATIONS

Design the marketplace from both sides.

Problem
Buyer trust collapses if sellers cannot reliably manage inventory, orders and payouts.
Constraint
Operational depth must not turn the shopping experience into an admin tool.
Decision
Inventory variants, orders, store profile, wallet and earnings were designed as one seller operating system.
Evidence
These seller capabilities are documented in the current public app-store release notes.

06What shipped

The live product now spans customer shopping and seller operations. Current public app-store notes describe product listing and stock variants, seller wallet and earnings, order management, store profile and location, KYC and store verification, and in-app chat with image sharing. Google Play also documents verified vendors, escrow-protected transactions and Paystack-powered Naira payments.

07Live proof

Horal is available as a live website and on both major mobile stores. That matters for this case study because the work is not presented as a concept: the buyer and seller flows are shipping product surfaces that continue to evolve through live releases.
